title: Vayigash: the wagons (Genesis 45:26–28)
hook: Jacob can't believe it until he sees the wagons, then his spirit revives

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's advice for the ride home: don't fall out on the way. Today the brothers arrive, and they have to tell their father the news.

Some news is too good to believe. The phone call that says the test came back clear. The text from someone you thought you'd lost touch with forever. Your first reaction isn't joy. It's: no, that can't be right. Now picture an old man who has grieved a son for over twenty years. He was shown a bloody coat. He said he'd go down to his grave mourning. And his sons walk in and say: Joseph is alive. He's the ruler of all Egypt.
screen: `TOO GOOD TO BELIEVE.` → `AN OLD MAN AND A BLOODY COAT.` → `JOSEPH IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: The first reaction, the text says, is that Jacob's heart went numb. He didn't believe them. Words weren't enough. So the brothers tell him everything Joseph said. Then he sees the wagons Joseph had sent from Egypt to carry him down. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "the spirit of Jacob their father revived." Then he speaks. "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive; I will go and see him before I die." Why the wagons? The rabbis noticed a pun. The Hebrew for wagons, agalot, sounds like eglah, a young cow. Rashi passes on a tradition that the last thing Jacob and Joseph studied together, before Joseph vanished, was a passage about a heifer. So the wagons were a private signal only a father would understand: it's really me, and I remember. Later storytellers add a tender scene the Torah doesn't have: Asher's daughter, Serach, breaks the news to her grandfather gently, in a song, so the shock won't hurt him. The Torah itself is silent about how they told him. And watch one small thing. In the verse where his spirit revives, he's still Jacob. In the very next verse, when he decides to go, the text calls him Israel, his larger name. Rashi adds that the presence of God, which had left him in his grief, came back. Sometimes good news needs to be seen before it can be believed. And sometimes the person delivering it matters as much as the news.
screen: `HIS HEART WENT NUMB.` · `THEN HE SAW THE WAGONS.` · `AGALOT — A SIGNAL FROM A SON.` · `JACOB BECOMES ISRAEL AGAIN.` · then, large: `HIS SPIRIT REVIVED.`

segments.voice: Think of one piece of good news you're holding that someone else would love to hear: a thank-you you haven't passed on, a compliment said behind their back, their kid did well, the thing they worried about worked out. Picture their face when they hear it, and decide how and when you'll tell them; sooner is kinder.
Vayigash. The portion where Jacob hears his lost son is alive, sees the wagons, and his spirit comes back to life.
Your line: his spirit revived. Words weren't enough; the wagons were. See you on day two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition has blessings for news: on hearing good news that benefits others too, many say the blessing praising God who is good and does good, and on hard news they say the blessing for the true Judge.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 45:27 and 45:28.
Rashi on 45:27: the eglah arufah signal and the return of the Shechinah, from memory (Rashi draws on Genesis Rabbah 94:3); confirm.
The Serach bat Asher harp/song story is from later sources (Sefer HaYashar and others); presented as a later story, confirm framing.
Blessings in howItsDone (HaTov v'HaMeitiv, Dayan HaEmet) described loosely; confirm.
Audit (10% sample): the teach said the text 'stops calling him Jacob' after 45:27, which overstates it (he is Jacob again in 46:2 and 46:5); reworded to say the next verse, 45:28, calls him Israel.
